name: Globalization
scope: Globalization as the defining sources present it: the process of growing worldwide integration and interdependence of economies, politics and cultures (Stanford Encyclopedia, Britannica, IMF), and the position of those who welcome it and want it extended: freer trade and capital movement, open markets and supranational institutions, with the reform-minded strand (Stiglitz) and the cosmopolitan strand (Held, Habermas) that want it managed or democratised. The sources present it as contested between its proponents and its opponents (the anti-globalization movement, nationalists, populists). Excluded: the opposing positions (critics answer nothing), globalism in Steger's sense and the antisemitic use of 'globalist' (own entries), and the alter- and anti-globalization movements (own entries).

summary: Globalization names the growing integration of the world's economies, politics and cultures, and the case for it. Its defenders (Bhagwati, Wolf, the IMF) hold that open trade and capital flows raise growth and cut poverty; reformers such as Stiglitz want it managed so it works for the poor, and cosmopolitans want global democratic institutions to match it. Nationalists, populists and the anti-globalization movement oppose it.
